items.why: Donor units are tested by a method that detects weak D because even weakly expressed D antigen can immunize a D-negative recipient. A donor whose cells react only in the weak D test is therefore **labeled D-positive**, so the unit will not be given to D-negative patients.

whyNot.0: Labeling the unit D-negative could expose a D-negative recipient to D antigen and cause anti-D formation; treating weak D as D-negative applies to some patients, not to donors.
whyNot.1: There is no separate weak D label for donor units; the unit is simply labeled D-positive.
whyNot.2: A weak D donor is a healthy donor, and the unit is fully usable for D-positive recipients.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.; Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter (weak D testing of donors). Value per AABB Standards; PH DOH/NVBSP may specify their own.

items.stem: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery in 3 weeks wants to donate autologous blood. AABB sets a minimum hemoglobin of 11 g/dL for autologous donors. Which finding should defer her from donating today?
options: A current bacterial infection with fever
An age of 74 years
A hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dL
An autologous unit collected 7 days earlier
items.why: Autologous donors may be older, smaller, or more anemic than allogeneic donors, and many criteria are relaxed. A key exclusion is **any condition that could cause bacteremia**, because bacteria that enter the unit can multiply during storage and cause a septic reaction when the blood is returned to the patient.

whyNot.1: There is no upper age limit for autologous donation; the patient's physician decides whether she can tolerate collection.
whyNot.2: A hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dL meets the 11 g/dL minimum stated in the question.
whyNot.3: Autologous donors may give more often than allogeneic donors, as long as the hemoglobin requirement is met and the last collection is at least 72 hours before surgery.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.; Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., donor selection chapter (autologous donation). Value per AABB Standards; PH DOH/NVBSP may specify their own.

items.stem: A whole blood bag designed for 450 mL of blood with 63 mL of anticoagulant is removed from the donor after only 330 mL has been collected. The red cells may be kept as a low-volume unit, but plasma and platelets should not be prepared from it. Why?
options: There is too little citrate to stop the unit from clotting
Adenine is too dilute to preserve the coagulation factors
The plasma contains too much citrate for its volume
Underfilled bags are more often contaminated by skin bacteria
items.why: The anticoagulant volume in the bag is set for a full collection, so a short draw leaves **an abnormally high ratio of anticoagulant to blood**. Plasma from such a unit is diluted and carries excess citrate, so only the red cells are used, labeled as a low-volume unit.

whyNot.0: An underfilled bag has relatively more anticoagulant, not less; clotting is a concern with overfilled bags.
whyNot.1: Adenine supports red cell ATP production and has no role in preserving coagulation factors in plasma.
whyNot.3: Bacterial contamination comes mainly from donor skin or bacteremia and does not depend on how full the bag is.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed. (low-volume units); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., donor collection and blood preservation chapters. Value per AABB Standards; PH DOH/NVBSP may specify their own.

items.stem: Red cells frozen with a high concentration of glycerol are deglycerolized before transfusion by washing with saline solutions of decreasing concentration (for example, 12%, then 1.6%, then 0.9% NaCl). This stepwise approach is used mainly to:
options: Prevent osmotic lysis of glycerol-loaded red cells
Restore 2,3-DPG lost during frozen storage
Remove cold agglutinins bound during freezing
Warm the cells slowly to avoid cold hemolysis
items.why: Glycerol enters the red cells during freezing. If thawed cells were placed directly in isotonic saline, water would rush into the glycerol-laden cells and lyse them, so **glycerol is removed gradually by stepping down the external osmolality**. The washing also removes most plasma, leukocytes, and free hemoglobin.

whyNot.1: Frozen storage essentially halts metabolism, so 2,3-DPG is preserved at about its level at the time of freezing rather than lost.
whyNot.2: Freezing does not cause cold agglutinins to bind, and saline washing steps are not designed to remove antibodies from the cells.
whyNot.3: Thawing is done separately in a 37 °C water bath or dry warmer; the saline series addresses osmotic stress, not temperature.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., blood preservation chapter (frozen red cells); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: A 2.0-kg neonate has a hematocrit of 24%. The neonatologist wants to raise it to 39% using a red cell unit with a hematocrit of 60%. Assuming a blood volume of 90 mL/kg, about how much of the unit should be transfused?
options: 27 mL
69 mL
45 mL
117 mL
items.why: Blood volume = 2.0 kg × 90 mL/kg = 180 mL. Volume to transfuse = blood volume × (desired Hct − current Hct) ÷ Hct of the unit = 180 × (39 − 24) ÷ 60 = **45 mL**.

whyNot.0: 27 mL (180 × 0.15) forgets to divide by the unit hematocrit, as if the unit were pure red cells.
whyNot.1: 69 mL divides by the desired hematocrit (39%) instead of the hematocrit of the unit (60%).
whyNot.3: 117 mL multiplies by the desired hematocrit (39%) instead of the needed rise of 15 percentage points.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., blood component therapy chapter (neonatal and pediatric transfusion); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

worked.problem: A 3.0-kg infant has a hematocrit of 28%. The goal is a hematocrit of 40%, and the red cell unit has a hematocrit of 70%. Assume a blood volume of 85 mL/kg. How much should be transfused?
steps: Estimate blood volume: 3.0 kg × 85 mL/kg = 255 mL.
Find the needed rise in hematocrit: 40% − 28% = 12 percentage points.
Volume = blood volume × rise ÷ unit Hct = 255 × 12 ÷ 70 = 43.7 mL.

items.stem: Prestorage leukoreduction of red cells and platelets is used mainly to reduce the risk of:
options: Graft-versus-host disease in immunocompromised recipients
Anaphylaxis in IgA-deficient patients who have anti-IgA
Circulatory overload in patients with heart failure
Febrile reactions, HLA alloimmunization, and CMV transmission
items.why: Filtering out white cells soon after collection removes the leukocytes whose cytokines and HLA antigens cause **febrile nonhemolytic reactions and HLA alloimmunization**, a major cause of platelet refractoriness. Because CMV resides in leukocytes, leukoreduction also lowers the risk of CMV transmission.

whyNot.0: The few viable lymphocytes left after filtration can still cause TA-GVHD; irradiation is used to prevent it.
whyNot.1: Leukoreduction does not remove plasma proteins such as IgA; washed or IgA-deficient components are needed.
whyNot.2: Circulatory overload depends on the volume and rate of transfusion, which leukoreduction does not change.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., blood component preparation chapter (leukocyte reduction); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman with heart failure receives 2 red cell units over 3 hours. Near the end of the second unit she becomes short of breath, with a blood pressure of 182/100 mm Hg, distended neck veins, and bilateral crackles. Her BNP is much higher than before transfusion, and she improves after intravenous furosemide. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)
Anaphylactic transfusion reaction
Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
items.why: TACO occurs when the volume or rate of transfusion exceeds what the circulation can handle, causing hydrostatic pulmonary edema; elderly patients and those with cardiac or renal disease are at highest risk. **Hypertension, a rising BNP, and a prompt response to diuretics** point to volume overload rather than TRALI.

whyNot.0: TRALI is a noncardiogenic, permeability edema that typically causes hypotension and fever and does not improve with diuretics.
whyNot.2: Anaphylaxis presents with hypotension, bronchospasm, and often urticaria, not hypertension with distended neck veins.
whyNot.3: An acute hemolytic reaction causes fever, chills, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, and pain rather than isolated volume overload that responds to diuretics.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: A patient who received 2 red cell units 3 weeks ago now needs another transfusion. Under AABB Standards, which sample is acceptable for the antibody screen and crossmatch?
options: A sample collected no more than 3 days before the transfusion
A sample collected no more than 7 days before the transfusion
The sample that was tested for the transfusion 3 weeks ago
Any sample collected during the patient's current admission
items.why: Transfusion or pregnancy within the past 3 months can stimulate new or anamnestic antibodies that appear within days. For these patients AABB requires **a sample collected within 3 days of the scheduled transfusion** (the day of collection is day 0), so testing reflects the antibodies currently present.

whyNot.1: A 7-day-old sample could miss an antibody that has formed since collection in a recently transfused patient.
whyNot.2: A sample taken before the last transfusion cannot detect antibodies stimulated by those red cells.
whyNot.3: An admission can last weeks, and an older sample from it may not reflect newly formed antibodies.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed. (pretransfusion sample requirements); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., compatibility testing chapter. Value per AABB Standards; PH DOH/NVBSP may specify their own.

items.stem: A DAT with polyspecific AHG is ordered for a patient with suspected cold agglutinin disease. Why is a sample collected in EDTA preferred over a clotted sample?
options: EDTA keeps bound IgG from eluting off the cells during storage
EDTA inactivates cold autoantibodies so they cannot agglutinate
Fibrin in clotted samples neutralizes the antiglobulin reagent
EDTA chelates calcium and blocks in vitro complement binding
items.why: Cold autoantibodies can bind red cells as a clotted sample cools and activate complement, coating the cells with C3 in the tube. Complement activation needs calcium and magnesium, so **EDTA prevents this in vitro C3 uptake**, and a positive DAT then reflects coating that occurred in the patient.

whyNot.0: EDTA has no effect on whether IgG dissociates from red cells; its value lies in stopping complement activation.
whyNot.1: EDTA does not inactivate antibodies; cold autoantibodies can still bind, but without calcium they cannot activate complement.
whyNot.2: AHG is neutralized by unbound serum globulin left after inadequate washing, not by fibrin.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., antiglobulin test chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed. (DAT specimen requirements)

items.stem: Compared with HDFN caused by anti-D, HDFN caused by ABO antibodies:
options: Usually causes severe anemia and hydrops fetalis
Typically gives a strongly positive DAT on cord cells
Can occur in a first pregnancy, mainly with group O mothers
Can be prevented with antenatal Rh immune globulin
items.why: Group O people often have IgG anti-A,B formed without prior red cell exposure, so **ABO HDFN can occur in a first pregnancy**. It is usually mild, with a weak or negative DAT, because A and B antigens are poorly developed on fetal red cells and A and B substances in fetal tissues absorb much of the antibody.

whyNot.0: ABO HDFN is usually mild, needing at most phototherapy; hydrops is characteristic of severe anti-D disease.
whyNot.1: The DAT in ABO HDFN is often weak or negative because fetal cells carry few A and B sites.
whyNot.3: Rh immune globulin contains only anti-D and prevents D alloimmunization; it has no effect on ABO antibodies.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: A 4-year-old develops sudden hemoglobinuria and anemia one week after a viral upper respiratory infection. The DAT is positive with anti-C3d only. When his serum and group O red cells are incubated first at 4 °C and then at 37 °C, hemolysis occurs; no hemolysis occurs in a tube kept only at 37 °C. The antibody most likely is:
options: A monophasic IgM with anti-I specificity
A biphasic IgG with anti-P specificity
A warm-reactive IgG with Rh-related specificity
A cold-reactive IgM with anti-i specificity
items.why: This is paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria. The **Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG hemolysin with anti-P specificity**: it binds red cells and fixes early complement components in the cold, and the cells lyse when warmed to 37 °C. Because the IgG dissociates at warm temperatures, the DAT usually shows only C3.

whyNot.0: Anti-I of cold agglutinin disease is IgM and does not require the cold-then-warm sequence; it usually follows Mycoplasma infection in adults.
whyNot.2: Warm autoantibodies react at 37 °C without a cold phase and usually give a DAT positive for IgG.
whyNot.3: Anti-i is associated with infectious mononucleosis and is IgM; it does not produce the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner pattern.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., autoimmune hemolytic anemias chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: Lysozyme, found in tears, saliva, and neutrophil granules, protects against bacteria by:
options: Binding iron so that bacteria cannot use it for growth
Coating bacteria so that phagocytes can ingest them
Hydrolyzing the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls
Neutralizing toxins that bacteria release into tissues
items.why: Lysozyme **cleaves the β-1,4 bonds between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine in peptidoglycan**, weakening the cell wall so the bacterium lyses. Gram-positive bacteria, with their thick and exposed peptidoglycan layer, are the most susceptible.

whyNot.0: Iron sequestration is the role of lactoferrin and transferrin, not lysozyme.
whyNot.1: Opsonization is performed by complement fragments such as C3b and by IgG antibodies.
whyNot.3: Toxin neutralization is a function of specific antibodies (antitoxins), not of lysozyme.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., natural (innate) immunity chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, innate immunity chapter

items.stem: Lipopolysaccharide from gram-negative bacteria is recognized by innate immune cells mainly through which pattern-recognition receptor?
options: Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3)
Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5)
Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)
Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)
items.why: **TLR4, together with MD-2 and CD14, recognizes the lipid A portion of LPS** on macrophages and dendritic cells. The resulting release of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α contributes to the fever and shock of gram-negative sepsis.

whyNot.0: TLR3 is an endosomal receptor for double-stranded viral RNA.
whyNot.1: TLR5 recognizes flagellin, the protein of bacterial flagella.
whyNot.3: TLR9 is an endosomal receptor for unmethylated CpG motifs in bacterial and viral DNA.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., natural (innate) immunity chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, innate immunity chapter

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had recurrent Staphylococcus aureus abscesses and an Aspergillus pneumonia. His neutrophil count is normal. In the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test, his stimulated neutrophils fail to reduce the yellow dye to dark blue formazan. Which component is defective?
options: Phagocyte NADPH oxidase
The CD18 β2-integrin for neutrophil adhesion
The LYST protein for lysosomal trafficking
Bruton tyrosine kinase in developing B cells
items.why: This is chronic granulomatous disease. Without functional NADPH oxidase, neutrophils cannot generate superoxide in the respiratory burst, so they ingest catalase-positive organisms but cannot kill them; **failure to reduce NBT reflects the absent respiratory burst**.

whyNot.1: CD18 deficiency (leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1) impairs neutrophil migration into tissues, but the respiratory burst and NBT reduction are normal.
whyNot.2: LYST defects cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome, with giant granules and partial albinism; the NBT test is normal.
whyNot.3: Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a B-cell disorder in which neutrophil killing is normal.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., immunodeficiency chapter (phagocytic defects); Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, primary immunodeficiencies chapter

items.stem: Which substance, injected into a rabbit, is most likely to be strongly immunogenic?
options: Albumin purified from the same rabbit's own serum
A 150-kDa glycoprotein purified from horse serum
A 1-kDa synthetic peptide given without any carrier
A large polymer made of one repeating amino acid
items.why: Strong immunogens are **foreign to the host, large (generally above about 100 kDa), and chemically complex**, and proteins are the most effective. A horse glycoprotein meets all of these conditions in a rabbit.

whyNot.0: The rabbit's own albumin is self, and tolerance normally prevents a response to it.
whyNot.2: A 1-kDa peptide is too small to be immunogenic by itself; it acts like a hapten unless coupled to a carrier.
whyNot.3: A homopolymer of a single amino acid lacks chemical complexity and is a poor immunogen regardless of its size.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., antigens and antibodies chapter (immunogenicity); Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, antigens and antibodies chapter

items.stem: Gm markers are inherited amino acid differences in the constant region of IgG heavy chains that vary from one person to another within the same species. Such variants are classified as:
options: Isotypes
Allotypes
Idiotypes
Paratopes
items.why: Allotypes are **allelic variants that differ among individuals of the same species**, such as Gm markers on γ heavy chains and Km markers on κ light chains. They are inherited codominantly and can stimulate antibodies after transfusion or pregnancy.

whyNot.0: Isotypes are the heavy-chain classes and subclasses (and κ and λ light chains) present in every normal member of a species.
whyNot.2: Idiotypes are unique determinants in the variable region of a particular antibody, related to its antigen-binding site.
whyNot.3: A paratope is the antigen-binding site of an antibody itself, not an inherited constant-region marker.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., immunoglobulins chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, immunoglobulin structure chapter

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent sinopulmonary infections and Pneumocystis pneumonia. His serum IgM is elevated, but IgG, IgA, and IgE are very low, and his B cells are present in normal numbers. The most likely defect is in:
options: Bruton tyrosine kinase in pre-B cells
CD40 ligand on activated helper T cells
The common gamma chain of cytokine receptors
Thymic development from the pharyngeal pouches
items.why: Class switching from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE requires helper T cells to engage CD40 on B cells through **CD40 ligand (CD154)**; without it, B cells continue to make only IgM. X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome also weakens T-cell activation of macrophages, which explains the susceptibility to Pneumocystis.

whyNot.0: Bruton tyrosine kinase defects block B-cell maturation, so B cells are nearly absent and all immunoglobulin classes, including IgM, are low.
whyNot.2: Common gamma chain defects cause X-linked SCID, with absent T and NK cells and low levels of all immunoglobulins rather than raised IgM.
whyNot.3: DiGeorge syndrome is a T-cell deficiency from thymic hypoplasia with hypocalcemia; immunoglobulin levels are usually near normal.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., immunodeficiency chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, primary immunodeficiencies chapter

items.stem: Which cytokine, produced mainly by Th2 cells, induces B cells to switch to IgE production?
options: Interferon-gamma
Interleukin-4
Interleukin-17
Interleukin-2
items.why: Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. **IL-4 drives B cells to class switch to IgE**, linking Th2 responses to allergy and to defense against helminths.

whyNot.0: Interferon-gamma is the Th1 cytokine; it promotes opsonizing IgG and suppresses IgE switching.
whyNot.2: IL-17 is made by Th17 cells and recruits neutrophils; it does not direct IgE class switching.
whyNot.3: IL-2 is mainly a T-cell growth factor that drives T-cell proliferation.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., cells of the immune system and cytokines chapters; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, cytokines chapter

items.stem: Regulatory T cells, which suppress immune responses and help maintain self-tolerance, are identified by expression of CD4, CD25, and which transcription factor?
options: FOXP3
T-bet
GATA-3
RORγt
items.why: **FOXP3 is the master transcription factor of regulatory T cells**, which suppress other lymphocytes in part through IL-10 and TGF-β. Mutations in FOXP3 cause IPEX syndrome, a severe autoimmune disease affecting many organs.

whyNot.1: T-bet directs differentiation of Th1 cells, which produce interferon-gamma.
whyNot.2: GATA-3 directs differentiation of Th2 cells, which produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.
whyNot.3: RORγt directs differentiation of Th17 cells, which produce IL-17.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., cells of the immune system chapter (T-cell subsets); Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, T cells chapter

items.stem: A woman awaiting a kidney transplant, who has had three pregnancies and several transfusions, has a calculated panel reactive antibody (cPRA) of 95%. This result means that she:
options: Shares about 95% of her HLA antigens with her intended donor
Has about a 95% chance that her graft will survive one year
Has HLA antibodies against about 95% of potential donors
Has serum that killed 95% of her intended donor's lymphocytes
items.why: PRA estimates the proportion of a donor population carrying HLA antigens to which the patient has antibodies; cPRA calculates it from the patient's identified HLA antibodies and population HLA frequencies. Pregnancy, transfusion, and earlier transplants sensitize patients, and **a high cPRA means few donors will give a negative crossmatch**.

whyNot.0: PRA measures antibodies against a population, not the degree of HLA matching with one donor.
whyNot.1: PRA is a measure of sensitization and is not a graft-survival estimate; highly sensitized patients actually face higher rejection risk.
whyNot.3: Killing of a specific donor's lymphocytes is the result of a crossmatch with that donor, not a PRA.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., transplantation immunology chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, transplantation chapter (HLA antibody testing)

items.stem: A man has a rash on his palms and soles and condylomata lata. His undiluted serum gives a nonreactive RPR result, but the same serum is clearly reactive when diluted 1:8. This pattern is best explained by:
options: A prozone caused by antibody excess
A postzone caused by antigen excess
A biologic false-positive reaction
Early primary syphilis before reagin forms
items.why: Secondary syphilis produces very high reagin titers. In undiluted serum the antibody can so outnumber the cardiolipin antigen particles that the lattice needed for visible flocculation does not form, a **prozone** effect; diluting the serum restores the antibody-antigen balance.

whyNot.1: A postzone reflects too little antibody relative to antigen; diluting the serum would make it worse, not reveal reactivity.
whyNot.2: A biologic false positive describes reactivity in a person without syphilis; here the patient has signs of secondary syphilis and the problem is a falsely nonreactive result.
whyNot.3: If reagin had not yet formed, the serum would stay nonreactive when diluted, and the clinical features here are those of secondary syphilis.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., syphilis serology chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, syphilis chapter

items.stem: In the Widal test for typhoid fever, which antigen of Salmonella Typhi is located on the flagella?
options: O antigen
Vi antigen
Fimbrial antigen
H antigen
items.why: **The H antigen is the flagellar protein**; antibodies against it give loose, floccular agglutination and tend to persist longer after infection or vaccination. The O antigen is the somatic LPS side chain, and anti-O gives compact, granular agglutination.

whyNot.0: The O antigen is the somatic (cell wall) lipopolysaccharide antigen, not a flagellar one.
whyNot.1: Vi is a capsular polysaccharide antigen of S. Typhi; it is not one of the antigens on the flagella.
whyNot.2: Fimbriae (pili) are adhesion structures distinct from flagella, and they are not the H antigen used in the Widal test.

items.ref: Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, serology of bacterial infections chapter; Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., bacterial serology chapter

items.stem: In a patient with chronic hepatitis B, a positive HBeAg indicates:
options: Immunity to HBV from a past infection
A successful response to hepatitis B vaccine
Resolution of infection with loss of HBsAg
Active viral replication and high infectivity
items.why: HBeAg is a soluble viral protein released during active replication, so its presence correlates with **high levels of circulating virus and high infectivity**. Seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe usually signals reduced replication, although precore mutant strains can replicate without making HBeAg.

whyNot.0: Immunity from past infection is shown by anti-HBs together with anti-HBc, with HBsAg negative.
whyNot.1: Vaccine response is shown by anti-HBs alone; the vaccine contains only HBsAg and does not produce HBeAg.
whyNot.2: Resolution is marked by loss of HBsAg and HBeAg with appearance of antibodies, not by a positive HBeAg.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., viral hepatitis chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, hepatitis chapter

items.stem: A patient in Metro Manila has had high fever, headache, and myalgia for 2 days, and dengue is suspected. Assuming this is a primary (first) dengue infection, which test is most likely to be positive this early?
options: Dengue IgM antibody
Dengue NS1 antigen
Dengue IgG antibody
Fourfold rise in hemagglutination-inhibition titer
items.why: NS1 is a nonstructural viral protein secreted into the blood from the first day of fever and usually detectable through the first week, **before antibodies are reliably present**. In a primary infection IgM becomes detectable in most patients only from about day 5 of illness and IgG later still, so an early negative antibody test does not exclude dengue.

whyNot.0: IgM is often not yet detectable on day 2 of a primary infection; it is most useful from about day 5 onward.
whyNot.2: In a primary infection IgG appears late, after IgM, and is not expected on day 2.
whyNot.3: A fourfold rise requires paired acute and convalescent samples taken weeks apart, so it cannot be positive this early.

items.ref: WHO, Dengue: Guidelines for Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention and Control (2009), laboratory diagnosis chapter; Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., viral infections chapter

items.stem: A man with fever and right upper quadrant pain has a single liver abscess. Aspiration yields odorless, brownish 'anchovy paste' material with no bacteria on Gram stain, and three stool examinations are negative for parasites. Which test best supports the suspected diagnosis?
options: Serum antibody to Echinococcus granulosus
Stool antigen test for Giardia duodenalis
Toxoplasma gondii IgG avidity testing
Serum antibody to Entamoeba histolytica
items.why: Anchovy-paste aspirate is classic for amebic liver abscess, and trophozoites are often absent from stool by that stage. Invasive amebiasis produces a strong antibody response, so **serum anti-E. histolytica antibodies are found in most patients with amebic liver abscess**; because antibodies can persist for years, results are interpreted with the clinical picture, especially in endemic areas.

whyNot.0: Echinococcus causes hydatid cysts containing clear fluid and hydatid sand, not anchovy-paste material.
whyNot.1: Giardia infects the small intestine and does not cause liver abscess, so a Giardia stool antigen would not address this lesion.
whyNot.2: Toxoplasma avidity testing dates a Toxoplasma infection, mainly in pregnancy, and is unrelated to liver abscess.

items.ref: Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, parasitic infections chapter; Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., serology of parasitic infections

items.stem: A patient with biopsy-proven pancreatic adenocarcinoma has an undetectable CA 19-9. Which red cell phenotype best explains why this marker cannot be used to monitor her disease?
options: Le(a−b−), lacking the Lewis fucosyltransferase
Le(a+b−), a nonsecretor of ABH substances
Group O, lacking the A and B transferases
P2 phenotype, lacking the P1 antigen
items.why: CA 19-9 is the sialylated Lewis a carbohydrate (sialyl-Lea). People who are Le(a−b−) (genotype lele) lack the Lewis fucosyltransferase (FUT3), so **they cannot make CA 19-9 even when a tumor is present**, giving falsely low results; this phenotype is found in a minority of people and is more common in those of African ancestry.

whyNot.1: Le(a+b−) nonsecretors still have the Lewis enzyme and make Lea structures, so they can produce CA 19-9.
whyNot.2: CA 19-9 is built on the Lewis pathway, not on A or B sugars, so group O does not prevent its synthesis.
whyNot.3: The P1 antigen belongs to an unrelated glycosphingolipid system and has no role in CA 19-9 synthesis.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Lewis blood group system chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, tumor markers chapter

items.stem: Serum protein electrophoresis on a 66-year-old man with bone pain shows a narrow band in the gamma region. Which test is used next to identify the heavy-chain and light-chain type of this protein?
options: Quantitative IgG, IgA, and IgM by nephelometry
Immunofixation electrophoresis
Heat precipitation test for Bence Jones protein
Serum viscosity measurement
items.why: Immunofixation separates serum proteins by electrophoresis and then overlays the lanes with antisera to γ, α, μ, κ, and λ chains. **A single sharp band with one heavy-chain and one light-chain antiserum** confirms a monoclonal protein and identifies its type, for example IgG κ.

whyNot.0: Nephelometry measures total immunoglobulin levels but cannot show whether an increase is monoclonal or which light chain is involved.
whyNot.2: The heat test detects free light chains in urine, is insensitive, and cannot identify a heavy chain or distinguish κ from λ.
whyNot.3: Viscosity assesses the risk of hyperviscosity syndrome and gives no information on the protein's identity.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., immunoproliferative diseases chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, monoclonal gammopathies chapter

items.stem: Measuring HIV viral load by RT-PCR requires an enzyme that copies the viral RNA into complementary DNA before amplification. That enzyme is:
options: Taq DNA polymerase
DNA ligase
Reverse transcriptase
Restriction endonuclease
items.why: PCR polymerases amplify DNA templates, so RNA targets such as HIV must first be copied into cDNA by **reverse transcriptase**, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase. The cDNA is then amplified and measured.

whyNot.0: Taq polymerase is the heat-stable DNA-dependent polymerase that amplifies the cDNA after it has been made.
whyNot.1: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments and is used in cloning, not to copy RNA.
whyNot.3: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific sequences and cannot make DNA from RNA.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., molecular diagnostic techniques chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, molecular techniques chapter

items.stem: For the daily quality control of anti-A typing reagent, which red cells serve as the positive and negative controls?
options: B cells positive; A1 cells negative
A1 cells positive; A2 cells negative
A1 cells positive; B cells negative
O cells positive; B cells negative
items.why: Each day of use, antisera are tested with cells that carry the target antigen and cells that lack it. For anti-A, **A1 cells should agglutinate and B cells should not**, confirming both reactivity and specificity.

whyNot.0: This reverses the controls; anti-A reacts with A1 cells, not B cells, and is the setup for anti-B.
whyNot.1: A2 cells carry A antigen and are agglutinated by anti-A, so they cannot serve as a negative control.
whyNot.3: Group O cells lack A antigen and would not react with anti-A, so they cannot be a positive control.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed. (reagent quality control); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., quality assurance chapter

items.stem: A regular blood donor tests positive for HCV on her latest donation, and the result is confirmed. The blood center then identifies her earlier donations, quarantines any in-date components, and arranges for recipients of her previous units to be notified. This process is called:
options: Traceback
Hemovigilance
Donor reentry
Lookback
items.why: **Lookback starts from an infected donor** and works forward to the components made from that donor's earlier donations and the patients who received them, so they can be tested and treated. It is a quality assurance requirement for transfusion-transmissible infections such as HIV and HCV.

whyNot.0: Traceback works in the opposite direction, from an infected recipient back to the donors of the units received.
whyNot.1: Hemovigilance is the overall surveillance system for adverse events across the transfusion chain, not this specific donor-to-recipient trace.
whyNot.2: Donor reentry is the process of requalifying a deferred donor after a falsely positive screening result.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed. (lookback); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., transfusion-transmitted diseases and quality assurance chapters

items.stem: A phlebotomist sticks herself with a needle that was just used to draw a patient's blood. What should she do first?
options: Wash the site with soap and water
Squeeze the wound to force out blood
Soak the site in undiluted bleach
Wait for the patient's test results
items.why: Immediate first aid is to **wash the puncture site with soap and water**, then report the exposure at once so the source patient can be tested and postexposure prophylaxis, if indicated, can start within hours.

whyNot.1: Squeezing the wound has not been shown to reduce infection risk and is not recommended.
whyNot.2: Bleach and other caustic agents damage the skin and are not recommended for wound care.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays reporting and prophylaxis, which work best when started as soon as possible.

items.ref: CDC/U.S. Public Health Service guidelines for occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, laboratory safety chapter

items.stem: Saliva from a healthy donor is tested by hemagglutination inhibition. It neutralizes anti-B and anti-H (Ulex europaeus) lectin, but it does not neutralize anti-A. Which description fits this donor?
options: Group O, carrying an Se gene
Group AB, carrying an Se gene
Group B, carrying an Se gene
Group B, genotype se/se
items.why: Secretors (Se gene, FUT2) put soluble ABH substances into saliva that match their ABO genes, always with H substance because H is the precursor for A and B. Inhibition of anti-B and anti-H but not anti-A shows B and H substances, so the donor is a **group B secretor**.

whyNot.0: A group O secretor's saliva has H substance only, so it would not neutralize anti-B.
whyNot.1: A group AB secretor's saliva also contains A substance and would neutralize anti-A.
whyNot.3: A nonsecretor (se/se) has no ABH substances in saliva, so neither anti-B nor anti-H would be neutralized.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., ABO blood group system chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A group A man and a group B woman have a group O first child. What is the chance that their next child will be group AB?
items.why: A group O child must receive an O gene from each parent, so the parents are genotypes AO and BO. Each child has a 1/2 chance of getting A from the father and a 1/2 chance of getting B from the mother, so the chance of AB is 1/2 x 1/2 = **25%**.

whyNot.1: 0% would be true only if one parent could not pass on A or B; both parents carry an expressed A or B gene.
whyNot.2: 50% is the chance that a child receives the A gene from the father (or B from the mother), not both at once.
whyNot.3: 75% is the chance that the child is NOT group O (1 - 1/4), not the chance of group AB.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., ABO blood group system and basic genetics chapters

items.stem: A patient with multiple myeloma types as follows (washed red cells): anti-A 0, anti-B 4+. His plasma gives 4+ with A1 cells and 2+ with B cells, group O screening cells, and his own cells at immediate spin. Under the microscope the clumps look like stacks of coins. Which procedure best resolves the reverse grouping?
options: Prewarming the plasma and cells to 37 °C
Saline replacement technique
Cold autoadsorption with the patient's own cells
Retesting the cells with anti-A1 lectin
items.why: Myeloma proteins cause rouleaux, which appear as stacked-coin aggregates in every tube that contains the patient's plasma, including the autocontrol. In the **saline replacement technique**, the plasma is removed after centrifugation and replaced with saline: rouleaux disperses, while true agglutination by anti-A or anti-B remains.

whyNot.0: Prewarming is used for cold-reacting autoantibodies or alloantibodies; it does not remove the plasma proteins that cause rouleaux.
whyNot.2: Cold autoadsorption removes cold autoantibodies such as anti-I; it does not help with excess plasma protein.
whyNot.3: Anti-A1 lectin helps find A subgroups in a forward-grouping problem, but this patient's discrepancy is in the reverse grouping.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., ABO blood group system chapter (ABO discrepancies); AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: In Wiener notation, which rare haplotype codes for C and E antigens but no D antigen?
options: Rz
r'
ry
items.why: Wiener uses an uppercase R for haplotypes that make D and a lowercase r for those that do not. A prime (') marks C, a double prime ('') marks E, and z or y marks C plus E together, so the haplotype dCE is written **ry** (r with a superscript y).

whyNot.0: Rz codes for D together with C and E (DCE), so it includes D.
whyNot.1: r' codes for C with e and no D (dCe); it does not make E.
whyNot.2: r'' codes for E with c and no D (dcE); it does not make C.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter (nomenclature)

items.stem: A woman's red cells react much more strongly with anti-D than R2R2 control cells do, and they give no reaction with anti-C, anti-c, anti-E, or anti-e. Her plasma contains an antibody that reacts with every panel cell tested. Her Rh phenotype is most likely:
options: Rh-null
Partial D
Weak D
items.why: In the **D-- phenotype**, the Rh gene makes no C/c or E/e antigens, and the cells carry more D antigen sites than any common phenotype, so they react with exalted strength. When immunized, these people often make antibody to a high-prevalence Rh antigen (such as anti-Hr0/Rh17) that reacts with all common red cells.

whyNot.1: Rh-null cells lack all Rh antigens, including D, so they would not react with anti-D.
whyNot.2: Partial D cells lack some D epitopes and usually type normally for C/c and E/e, not with stronger D.
whyNot.3: Weak D cells have fewer D sites and react more weakly than usual, the opposite of this finding.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A newly found antibody reacts with D-positive adult red cells but not with most D-negative adult cells. The lab suspects anti-LW rather than anti-D. Which finding best supports anti-LW?
options: Strong agglutination of Rh-null cells
Same strength with D-pos and D-neg cord cells
Reactivity confined to ficin-treated cells
A cold IgM agglutinin with no 37 °C activity
items.why: LW antigen is expressed more strongly on D-positive than on D-negative adult cells, so anti-LW can look like anti-D. On cord cells, however, LW is expressed equally whatever the D type, so **reactivity with D-negative cord cells** points to anti-LW.

whyNot.0: Rh-null cells lack LW as well as Rh antigens, so anti-LW does not react with them.
whyNot.2: LW antigens are not destroyed by ficin, and anti-LW does not react only with enzyme-treated cells.
whyNot.3: Anti-LW is usually IgG and is detected at the antiglobulin phase; temperature alone does not tell it apart from anti-D.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter (LW)

items.stem: An adult has inherited at least one Le gene but is homozygous se/se (nonsecretor). How will his red cells type for Lewis antigens?
options: Le(a-b+)
Le(a-b-)
Le(a+b-)
Le(a+b+)
items.why: The Le gene (FUT3) adds fucose to type 1 chains to make Lea. Making Leb also needs the Se gene (FUT2), which forms type 1 H; a nonsecretor cannot do this, so he types **Le(a+b-)**.

whyNot.0: Le(a-b+) needs both Le and Se; it is the usual phenotype of Lewis-positive secretors.
whyNot.1: Le(a-b-) occurs when no Le gene is inherited (le/le), whatever the secretor status.
whyNot.3: Le(a+b+) is a transient phenotype in infants (and a weak-secretor phenotype in some Asian populations), not expected in a se/se adult.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Lewis system chapter

items.stem: A Le(a-b+) red cell unit is transfused to a patient whose own cells type Le(a-b-). If samples are tested several days later, the donor cells in the patient's circulation will most likely type as:
options: Le(a-b-), because Lewis antigens move off the cells into the recipient's plasma
Le(a-b+), because Lewis antigens are fixed in the red cell membrane
Le(a+b-), because recipient enzymes convert Leb back to Lea
Le(a+b+), because the recipient's plasma adds Lea to the cells
items.why: Lewis antigens are not made by red cells; they are glycolipids that red cells take up from plasma, and they leave the cells as easily as they attach. Transfused Lewis-positive cells in a Lewis-negative recipient therefore **become Le(a-b-)**, and the antigen released into plasma can neutralize Lewis antibodies. This is one reason Lewis antibodies rarely cause hemolytic reactions.

whyNot.1: Lewis antigens are adsorbed from plasma, not built into the membrane like Rh or Kell proteins.
whyNot.2: There is no recipient enzyme that converts Leb to Lea; Leb is made by adding fucose, not by removing it.
whyNot.3: A Le(a-b-) recipient has no Lewis glycolipid in plasma to give to the cells.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Lewis system chapter

items.stem: Which red cell antigen survives ficin treatment but is destroyed when the cells are treated with 0.2 M dithiothreitol (DTT)?
options: Fya (Duffy)
M (MNS)
Jka (Kidd)
K (Kell)
items.why: Kell antigens sit on a glycoprotein held in shape by disulfide bonds, so reducing agents such as DTT and ZZAP denature them, while ficin and papain do not. **K** is therefore resistant to enzymes but sensitive to DTT. This is why DTT-treated cells cannot be used to detect anti-K.

whyNot.0: Fya is destroyed by ficin and papain, so it does not survive the enzyme treatment.
whyNot.1: M and N are also cleaved from glycophorin A by ficin and papain.
whyNot.2: Jka is resistant to ficin (its reactions are usually enhanced) and is not destroyed by DTT.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Other major blood group systems chapter (Kell); AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: The gene for which blood group system is on the X chromosome, so that its antigen is found more often in women than in men?
options: Duffy
Xg
Lutheran
Diego
items.why: The **Xg** gene is on the short arm of the X chromosome. Because women have two X chromosomes, they are Xg(a+) more often than men; Xg(a) frequency is about 89% in women and 66% in men of European descent.

whyNot.0: The Duffy gene is on chromosome 1 (autosomal), so frequencies do not differ by sex.
whyNot.2: The Lutheran gene is on chromosome 19 and is inherited autosomally.
whyNot.3: The Diego antigens are on band 3, encoded by a gene on chromosome 17.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Minor blood group systems chapter

items.stem: A patient's plasma gives weak (w+ to 1+) antiglobulin reactions with most panel cells. The reactivity is inhibited when the plasma is mixed with pooled plasma from normal donors, and it reacts strongly with red cells coated with C4. The most likely antibody is:
options: Anti-Kna (Knops)
Anti-Sda
Anti-Ch (Chido)
Anti-Vel
items.why: Chido/Rodgers antigens are carried on the C4 complement protein, which is present in plasma and adsorbed onto red cells. Because normal plasma contains the antigen, it neutralizes the antibody, and C4-coated cells react strongly; these findings identify **anti-Ch**, which is clinically insignificant.

whyNot.0: Knops antigens are on complement receptor 1 (CR1) of the red cell membrane and are not neutralized by plasma.
whyNot.1: Anti-Sda is neutralized by urine (especially guinea pig urine), not plasma, and gives refractile mixed-field agglutinates.
whyNot.3: Anti-Vel is a potent, often hemolytic antibody to a high-prevalence antigen and is not neutralized by plasma.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Minor blood group systems chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A prospective blood donor received a measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine 10 days ago. What is the correct donor decision?
options: Accept; vaccines never cause deferral
Defer; eligible 2 weeks from the vaccine date
Defer; eligible 12 months from the vaccine date
Defer; eligible 4 weeks from the vaccine date
items.why: Live attenuated vaccines can give a short-lived viremia. Vaccines containing rubella (alone or as MMR) call for a **4-week deferral** from the date of vaccination; under AABB criteria a 2-week deferral applies to some other live vaccines, such as measles or mumps given alone, while WHO guidance uses 4 weeks for all live attenuated vaccines.

whyNot.0: Toxoid and killed vaccines usually carry no deferral, but live vaccines such as MMR do.
whyNot.1: Under AABB criteria, two weeks is the deferral for some other live vaccines (for example, measles or mumps alone), not for rubella-containing vaccines such as MMR.
whyNot.2: A 12-month deferral is not linked to MMR; it applies to other exposures under some standards.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Donor screening and component preparation chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.); WHO Blood donor selection: guidelines on assessing donor suitability for blood donation

items.stem: Which donor history is a reason for permanent (indefinite) deferral from blood donation?
options: A confirmed positive HCV test on an earlier donation
Travel to a malaria-endemic area last year
A rubella vaccination 2 weeks ago
Gonorrhea diagnosed and fully treated earlier this year
items.why: A donor who has tested positive for HCV can carry the virus for life, so a **confirmed positive HCV result** leads to indefinite deferral. The donor is entered into the deferral registry so that later donations are not accepted.

whyNot.1: Malaria travel risk leads to a temporary deferral, after which the donor may give blood again.
whyNot.2: Rubella vaccination leads to a short, temporary deferral (4 weeks).
whyNot.3: Treated sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea lead to a temporary deferral, not a permanent one.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Donor screening and component preparation chapter; Transfusion-transmitted diseases chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Which test is NOT done routinely on every allogeneic blood donation?
options: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)
Antibody to cytomegalovirus (anti-CMV)
Antibody to hepatitis C virus (anti-HCV)
Serologic test for syphilis
items.why: HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV, and syphilis testing are required on every donation. **Anti-CMV** testing is optional; it is done only to supply CMV-seronegative units for at-risk patients, such as low-birth-weight infants and some transplant recipients, and leukoreduction is an accepted alternative.

whyNot.0: HBsAg testing is required on all allogeneic donations to prevent hepatitis B transmission.
whyNot.2: Anti-HCV testing (with nucleic acid testing where available) is required on all donations.
whyNot.3: Syphilis serology is still a required donor test.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Donor screening and component preparation chapter; Transfusion-transmitted diseases chapter

items.stem: A patient receives several red cell units that are near the end of their shelf life. Right after the transfusion, how does the 2,3-DPG content of these cells affect oxygen delivery?
options: Hemoglobin holds oxygen less tightly, so more oxygen is released to tissues
Oxygen release is unchanged, because 2,3-DPG does not affect hemoglobin
Hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly, so less oxygen is released to tissues
The oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right, improving delivery
items.why: 2,3-DPG falls during refrigerated storage. With less 2,3-DPG, the oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the left, so **hemoglobin oxygen affinity increases** and less oxygen is given up at tissue oxygen tensions. The cells rebuild 2,3-DPG after transfusion, mostly within about a day.

whyNot.0: Lower oxygen affinity would come from an increase in 2,3-DPG, which does not happen during storage.
whyNot.1: 2,3-DPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and is a major regulator of oxygen affinity.
whyNot.3: A right shift (lower affinity) is caused by higher 2,3-DPG, acidosis, or fever, not by stored cells low in 2,3-DPG.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Red blood cell and platelet preservation chapter

items.stem: A unit of rare red cells is near expiry. It is incubated at 37 °C with a solution of pyruvate, inosine, phosphate, and adenine before freezing. The purpose of this step is to:
options: Remove leukocytes from the unit
Kill bacteria that may have entered the unit
Act as the cryoprotective agent during freezing
Restore the cells' ATP and 2,3-DPG levels
items.why: Rejuvenation solutions such as this (PIPA, now sold as Rejuvesol) supply substrates that let stored red cells **regenerate ATP and 2,3-DPG**, bringing them close to fresh levels. The solution must be washed out before transfusion, usually during deglycerolization if the cells are frozen.

whyNot.0: Leukocytes are removed by filtration, not by a metabolic rejuvenation solution.
whyNot.1: Rejuvenation solutions are not antimicrobial; pathogen reduction uses other methods.
whyNot.2: The cryoprotective agent for red cells is glycerol, which is added separately.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Red blood cell and platelet preservation chapter

items.stem: Some red cell additive solutions, such as AS-1 and AS-5, contain mannitol. What does mannitol do?
options: Protects the membrane, reducing storage hemolysis
Supplies glucose to fuel red cell glycolysis
Binds calcium so the unit does not clot
Acts as the purine source for ATP synthesis
items.why: Additive solutions contain saline, dextrose, and adenine, and some also contain mannitol. **Mannitol protects the red cell membrane** and lowers storage hemolysis, which helps make the 42-day shelf life possible.

whyNot.1: Energy for glycolysis comes from the dextrose (glucose) in the solution.
whyNot.2: Calcium is chelated by the citrate in the primary anticoagulant (for example, CPD).
whyNot.3: Adenine, not mannitol, is the substrate red cells use to keep up their ATP.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Red blood cell and platelet preservation chapter

items.stem: A whole blood-derived platelet concentrate with a very high platelet count was stored in a small volume of plasma. At day 5 its pH is 5.9. What is the main cause of this fall in pH?
options: Breakdown of the citrate anticoagulant into citric acid
Lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis (too little oxygen)
Release of acid from lysed red cells in the concentrate
Too much oxygen entering through the gas-permeable bag
items.why: Stored platelets rely mainly on aerobic metabolism. When the platelet content is high compared with plasma volume and oxygen exchange through the bag, metabolism shifts to anaerobic glycolysis, and **lactic acid** uses up the plasma bicarbonate, so pH falls. Current AABB Standards require platelets to keep a pH of at least 6.2 at the end of storage, because lower pH damages their viability.

whyNot.0: Citrate is metabolized and does not break down into enough acid to lower the pH of the unit.
whyNot.2: Platelet concentrates contain very few red cells, and red cell lysis is not what lowers platelet pH.
whyNot.3: Oxygen entering the bag supports aerobic metabolism and helps keep the pH up; it does not lower it.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Red blood cell and platelet preservation chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A nurse wants to run a solution through the same IV line as a red cell unit. Which one is acceptable?
options: Ringer's lactate
D5W (dextrose only)
0.9% sodium chloride
0.45% sodium chloride
items.why: **Normal (0.9%) saline** is the only solution routinely approved to run with red cells. Fluids with calcium can overcome the citrate and cause clots, and hypotonic or dextrose-only fluids make the red cells swell and lyse.

whyNot.0: Lactated Ringer's contains calcium, which can reverse the citrate anticoagulant and form clots in the line.
whyNot.1: Dextrose in water causes red cells to clump and swell, and they can hemolyze.
whyNot.3: Half-normal saline is hypotonic and can cause osmotic hemolysis.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion therapy chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A neutropenic patient with a bacterial infection that is not responding to antibiotics is ordered an apheresis granulocyte concentrate. Which handling is correct?
options: Irradiate, crossmatch, and give it promptly with no leukocyte filter
Pass it through a leukocyte filter to remove the lymphocytes
Refrigerate it at 1–6 °C and use it within the next 5 days
Skip the crossmatch, since it contains almost no red cells
items.why: Granulocytes lose function quickly, so they are transfused as soon as possible (within 24 hours, stored at 20–24 °C). They are **irradiated** to prevent TA-GVHD, and they must be ABO-compatible and crossmatched because they contain a lot of red cells. A leukoreduction filter would remove the cells being transfused.

whyNot.1: A leukoreduction filter would remove the granulocytes themselves; irradiation, not filtration, prevents TA-GVHD here.
whyNot.2: Granulocytes are not refrigerated, and they cannot be kept for days.
whyNot.3: Granulocyte concentrates contain enough red cells to need ABO compatibility and a crossmatch.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion therapy chapter; Apheresis chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: For most therapeutic plasma exchanges, 5% albumin is the replacement fluid. For a patient with acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), plasma is used instead. Why?
options: Plasma carries fewer allergic reactions than albumin
Plasma supplies the ADAMTS13 enzyme the patient lacks
Plasma replaces the platelets used up in microthrombi
Plasma has a higher oncotic pressure than 5% albumin
items.why: In acquired TTP, an autoantibody inhibits ADAMTS13, the protease that cleaves large von Willebrand factor multimers. Plasma exchange removes the inhibitor, and replacing with plasma **gives back working ADAMTS13**; albumin would remove the inhibitor without replacing the enzyme.

whyNot.0: Plasma causes allergic and other reactions more often than albumin; it is chosen despite this.
whyNot.2: Plasma components contain essentially no functional platelets, and platelet transfusion is generally avoided in TTP.
whyNot.3: Oncotic pressure is not the reason; 5% albumin is roughly iso-oncotic with plasma.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Apheresis chapter

items.stem: A 70-kg bleeding patient has a fibrinogen of 80 mg/dL, and the target is 150 mg/dL. His hematocrit is 30%, and his blood volume is 70 mL/kg. If each unit of cryoprecipitate contains 250 mg of fibrinogen, about how many units are needed?
items.why: Blood volume = 70 x 70 = 4,900 mL; plasma volume = 4,900 x (1 - 0.30) = 3,430 mL = 34.3 dL. Fibrinogen needed = (150 - 80) x 34.3 = 2,401 mg; 2,401 / 250 = 9.6, so about **10 units**.

whyNot.1: 14 comes from using the whole blood volume (49 dL) and ignoring the hematocrit.
whyNot.2: 16 comes from assuming only 150 mg of fibrinogen per unit (the minimum quality-control value) instead of the 250 mg stated.
whyNot.3: 21 comes from multiplying the target level (150 mg/dL) by plasma volume, instead of the increase needed (70 mg/dL).

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion therapy chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

worked.problem: A 60-kg patient (blood volume 70 mL/kg, hematocrit 35%) has a fibrinogen of 100 mg/dL. How many cryoprecipitate units (200 mg fibrinogen each) are needed to reach 180 mg/dL?
steps: Blood volume = 60 kg x 70 mL/kg = 4,200 mL.
Fibrinogen needed = (180 - 100) mg/dL x 27.3 dL = 2,184 mg.
Units = 2,184 / 200 = 10.9; round up.

items.stem: A patient with an IgM antibody, which stays mostly inside the blood vessels, has a 1.5 plasma-volume plasma exchange. Assuming the removal follows a one-compartment model with no new synthesis and no redistribution during the procedure, about what percentage of the antibody is removed?
items.why: In a one-compartment exchange, the fraction left = e^(-V), where V is the number of plasma volumes exchanged. For V = 1.5, e^(-1.5) = 0.22, so about 22% remains and **about 78% is removed**. Each extra volume removes less than the one before, which is why the first plasma volume is the most efficient.

whyNot.0: 63% (1 - e^-1) is what a single plasma-volume exchange removes, not 1.5 volumes.
whyNot.2: 86% (1 - e^-2) would need a 2 plasma-volume exchange.
whyNot.3: Exchanging 1.5 plasma volumes does not remove everything, because returned fluid keeps diluting what is left.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Apheresis chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

worked.problem: What fraction of an intravascular substance remains after a 1.0 and after a 2.0 plasma-volume exchange (one-compartment model, no synthesis)?
steps: Use fraction remaining = e^(-V).
V = 1.0: e^(-1) = 0.37, so 37% remains (63% removed).
Doubling the volume exchanged adds only about 23 percentage points of removal.
worked.result: 37% remains after 1 volume; 13.5% remains after 2 volumes.

items.stem: A man with hemophilia B is bleeding into a joint. Which product directly replaces the missing factor?
options: Recombinant or plasma-derived factor VIII
Pooled cryo from several donors
A unit of apheresis platelets
Recombinant or plasma-derived factor IX
items.why: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is an X-linked deficiency of factor IX. Treatment is **factor IX concentrate** (recombinant or plasma-derived); prothrombin complex concentrates also contain factor IX.

whyNot.0: Factor VIII concentrate treats hemophilia A, not hemophilia B.
whyNot.1: Cryoprecipitate has factor VIII, fibrinogen, vWF, and factor XIII, but almost no factor IX.
whyNot.2: Platelet counts and function are normal in hemophilia B, so platelets would not help.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion therapy chapter

items.stem: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, the patient develops chills, back pain, and a fall in blood pressure. What should the nurse do first?
options: Halt the unit, then keep venous access with a 0.9% saline drip
Draw blood cultures through the line before doing anything else
Finish the unit quickly so the bag can be sent to the lab
Give an antihistamine and let the unit continue
items.why: When a hemolytic reaction is suspected, the first step is to **stop the transfusion at once and keep the IV open with saline** for treatment. Then the bedside identification is checked, the physician and blood bank are notified, and the bag and post-transfusion samples are sent for investigation.

whyNot.1: Samples are collected after the transfusion is stopped; any delay lets more incompatible blood enter, and the amount transfused relates to how severe the reaction is.
whyNot.2: Finishing the unit could give more incompatible blood and make the reaction worse.
whyNot.3: Antihistamines treat mild allergic (hives-only) reactions; these signs suggest hemolysis, so the transfusion must stop.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: During surgery under general anesthesia, soon after a red cell unit is started, the patient develops unexplained hypotension and new, diffuse oozing from the incision and IV sites. Which transfusion complication should be suspected first?
options: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
Febrile nonhemolytic reaction
Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
Mild allergic (urticarial) reaction
items.why: An anesthetized patient cannot report chills, back pain or anxiety, so an acute hemolytic reaction may first show as **unexplained hypotension and bleeding from DIC**; hemoglobinuria may also appear in the urine catheter bag. The unit should be stopped at once and a reaction workup started.

whyNot.0: Circulatory overload typically raises blood pressure and causes pulmonary edema, and it does not cause generalized oozing.
whyNot.1: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction causes fever and chills, not hypotension with abnormal bleeding.
whyNot.3: A mild allergic reaction causes hives and itching, without hypotension or bleeding.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter

items.stem: Midway through a plasma transfusion, a patient gets a few itchy hives on the arm. Vital signs are normal, and there is no wheezing or fever. What is the usual management?
options: End the unit and send samples for a hemolysis investigation
Discard the unit and give only washed products from now on
Keep the same rate, since hives need no action of any kind
Pause, give an antihistamine, and resume the unit if hives clear
items.why: Mild urticaria is caused by recipient antibodies (often IgE) reacting with donor plasma proteins. It is the one reaction where, after **pausing and giving an antihistamine**, the same unit may be restarted once the symptoms go away, and no laboratory workup is needed.

whyNot.0: A hemolytic workup is not needed for hives alone without fever, hypotension, or other signs.
whyNot.1: Washed products are kept for repeated or severe allergic or anaphylactic reactions, not one mild episode.
whyNot.2: The transfusion should still be paused to check the patient and treat the symptoms.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Nine days after a red cell transfusion, a 58-year-old woman with three earlier pregnancies has a platelet count of 4 x 10^9/L, along with widespread purpura and nosebleeds. Her own platelets lack the antigen her antibody targets. Which antibody is most likely responsible?
options: Antibody to HLA class I antigens
Anti-HPA-1a
Anti-IgA
Anti-Jka
items.why: This is post-transfusion purpura (PTP). It usually occurs about a week after transfusion in a woman sensitized by pregnancy, typically HPA-1a-negative, who makes **anti-HPA-1a**. For reasons not fully understood, her own antigen-negative platelets are also destroyed, so she has severe thrombocytopenia.

whyNot.0: HLA class I antibodies cause refractoriness to platelet transfusions, not sudden destruction of the patient's own platelets.
whyNot.2: Anti-IgA in IgA-deficient patients causes anaphylaxis during transfusion, not delayed thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.3: Anti-Jka causes delayed hemolytic reactions affecting red cells, not platelets.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Blood centers added nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HIV and HCV to donor antibody screening mainly to:
options: Replace antibody tests so each donation needs only one test
Screen platelet units for bacterial growth
Catch infections in the weeks before seroconversion
Show which donors are immune after vaccination
items.why: Antibodies take weeks to appear after infection, and units donated during this window can transmit virus despite a negative antibody test. NAT detects viral RNA directly, so it **shortens the window period** and lowers the remaining risk of transmission.

whyNot.0: NAT was added to antibody testing, not used in place of it; both are still performed.
whyNot.1: Bacterial contamination is detected by culture or rapid bacterial tests, not by viral NAT.
whyNot.3: There is no vaccine for HIV or HCV, and NAT detects the virus itself, not immunity.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion-transmitted diseases chapter

items.stem: Which set of conditions allows a hospital to use an electronic (computer) crossmatch instead of a serologic crossmatch?
options: A nonreactive DAT on today's specimen, with a single ABO typing
A negative immediate-spin crossmatch done within the past 7 days
A positive antibody screen that is due only to a cold antibody
No significant antibodies, current or historical, and two ABO determinations
items.why: An electronic crossmatch can replace the serologic one only when the recipient has **no current or past clinically significant antibodies**, and the ABO group has been determined on two occasions (one on the current sample). The computer system must also be validated on site and must block release of ABO-incompatible units.

whyNot.0: The DAT is not a requirement for electronic crossmatching and does not show whether the patient has alloantibodies.
whyNot.1: An electronic crossmatch replaces the serologic crossmatch; it is not based on an earlier immediate-spin test.
whyNot.2: A positive antibody screen, whatever its cause, needs further investigation and usually serologic crossmatching.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Pretransfusion compatibility testing chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A 6-week-old infant in the neonatal unit had ABO/D typing and a negative antibody screen on admission. She now needs her third red cell aliquot during the same admission. What pretransfusion testing is required?
options: No repeat screen or crossmatch this admission (under 4 months)
A full antiglobulin crossmatch with every new aliquot
Repeat ABO grouping, including reverse typing, on a new sample
A repeat antibody screen every 3 days, as for adult patients
items.why: Infants younger than 4 months rarely make alloantibodies. If the first antibody screen (on infant or maternal serum) is negative, **repeat crossmatching and antibody screening can be omitted** for the rest of that admission until the infant is 4 months old, which also reduces blood draws.

whyNot.1: A crossmatch is not required when the initial screen shows no unexpected antibodies.
whyNot.2: Reverse grouping is not done in young infants, because their anti-A and anti-B are absent or come from the mother.
whyNot.3: The 3-day sample rule is for recently transfused or pregnant patients who can make new antibodies; young infants are exempt.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Pretransfusion compatibility testing chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman who is group AB, D-negative needs red cells and plasma. The blood bank has no AB, D-negative red cells. Which combination is the best choice?
options: Group A, D-negative red cells with group A plasma
Group AB, D-positive red cells with group AB plasma
Group A, D-negative red cells with group AB plasma
Group O, D-negative red cells with group O plasma
items.why: A group AB patient has no anti-A or anti-B, so A, B, or O red cells are all ABO-compatible, and a D-negative woman of childbearing age should get D-negative red cells. Her plasma must be group AB, because plasma of any other group has anti-A and/or anti-B that would react with her cells. So the best choice is **A, D-negative red cells with AB plasma**.

whyNot.0: Group A plasma contains anti-B, which can hemolyze the patient's own AB red cells.
whyNot.1: D-positive red cells could immunize her to D and put future pregnancies at risk of HDFN.
whyNot.3: Group O plasma has both anti-A and anti-B and is incompatible with an AB recipient.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Pretransfusion compatibility testing chapter; Transfusion therapy chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A patient's records show anti-Jka found 4 years ago at another hospital. Today her antibody screen is negative. What is the correct way to choose red cells?
options: Jka-negative units, checked by immediate-spin crossmatch only
Jka-negative units, compatible by antiglobulin crossmatch
Jkb-negative units, compatible by antiglobulin crossmatch
Any ABO-compatible units, as the antibody has disappeared
items.why: Kidd antibodies often fall below detectable levels and come back quickly after re-exposure, causing delayed hemolytic reactions. Once a clinically significant antibody has been identified, the patient should always get **antigen-negative units compatible by antiglobulin crossmatch**, even if the current screen is negative.

whyNot.0: An immediate-spin crossmatch detects ABO incompatibility; the patient's history calls for a full antiglobulin crossmatch.
whyNot.2: The patient's antibody is anti-Jka, so the units must lack Jka; whether they lack Jkb does not matter.
whyNot.3: The antibody is only below detection; a Jka-positive unit could boost it and cause a delayed hemolytic reaction.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Pretransfusion compatibility testing chapter; Other major blood group systems chapter (Kidd); AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Eight days after receiving 3 units of red cells, a patient's DAT with anti-IgG shows small agglutinates scattered among many free red cells (mixed-field). The DAT before transfusion was negative. What does this pattern most likely mean?
options: A warm autoantibody is coating all of the patient's own red cells
An alloantibody is coating only the transfused donor red cells
Complement was bound in vitro because the sample was refrigerated
Poor washing let free globulin neutralize the antiglobulin reagent
items.why: A mixed-field DAT means two red cell populations are present and only one is coated. Soon after a transfusion, this usually means **a new or anamnestic alloantibody is coating only the transfused donor cells**, the picture of a delayed hemolytic or delayed serologic transfusion reaction; an eluate should be prepared to identify the antibody.

whyNot.0: An autoantibody coats the patient's own cells and usually the donor cells too, so the reaction would be uniform rather than mixed-field.
whyNot.2: In vitro complement uptake in a refrigerated clotted sample gives a C3d result, not IgG coating of part of the cell population.
whyNot.3: Poor washing neutralizes the AHG reagent and causes a false-negative result, not a mixed-field positive.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Antiglobulin test chapter; Adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: In a polyethylene glycol (PEG) antibody screen, the tubes are NOT centrifuged and read after the 37 °C incubation. Instead they go straight to washing. Why?
options: Spinning cells in PEG causes nonspecific clumping
PEG destroys IgM antibodies during the incubation
PEG adds salt and blocks agglutination at 37 °C
PEG itself works as the antiglobulin reagent
items.why: PEG removes water from the test system, which concentrates antibody near the red cells and increases antibody uptake. It also **makes cells aggregate nonspecifically** if they are centrifuged in it, so the tubes are washed and only the antiglobulin phase is read.

whyNot.1: PEG does not destroy IgM; the procedure avoids a 37 °C reading because of false aggregation.
whyNot.2: PEG is not used to raise ionic strength; it works by excluding water.
whyNot.3: AHG reagent must still be added after washing; PEG only enhances antibody binding.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Antiglobulin test chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: In a solid-phase red cell adherence antibody screen, reagent red cell membranes are fixed to the well. After patient plasma is incubated and the wells washed, anti-IgG-coated indicator cells are added and spun. A positive result looks like:
options: A tight button of indicator cells in the center of the well
Indicator cells spread as an even layer across the bottom of the well
Agglutinates trapped at the top of a gel column
Lysis of the indicator red cells in the well
items.why: If patient IgG has bound to the fixed membranes, the anti-IgG on the indicator cells binds to it, and the cells **adhere in a diffuse layer** across the well. If no IgG is bound, the indicator cells roll down and form a compact button in the center, which is a negative result.

whyNot.0: A compact central button means the indicator cells did not adhere, which is a negative result.
whyNot.2: Agglutinates trapped in a gel column are how column (gel) agglutination tests are read, not solid-phase adherence.
whyNot.3: Hemolysis is not the endpoint of solid-phase adherence testing.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Other technologies and automation in the blood bank chapter

items.stem: A tube LISS antibody screen calls for 2 drops of plasma and 2 drops of LISS. A trainee adds 4 drops of plasma instead. How does this most likely affect the test?
options: Even lower ionic strength results, with false-positive reactions
No effect, since more plasma always means more antibody
Higher ionic strength slows antibody uptake; weak antibodies may be missed
The antiglobulin phase is no longer needed to detect IgG
items.why: LISS works by lowering ionic strength, which reduces the shielding of charges around antigen and antibody and speeds up antibody uptake. Extra plasma (which has normal ionic strength) **raises the ionic strength of the mixture**, cancelling some of the enhancement, so a weak antibody may be missed within the short incubation time.

whyNot.0: Adding more plasma raises, not lowers, the ionic strength of the mixture.
whyNot.1: Extra antibody does not make up for the loss of the low-ionic environment, and the incubation time is set for the correct ratio.
whyNot.3: LISS enhances sensitization but does not replace the antiglobulin phase for detecting IgG.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Fundamentals of immunology for blood bankers chapter; Antiglobulin test chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia received red cells 2 weeks ago. Her plasma reacts with all panel cells, and her DAT is positive with anti-IgG. Which procedure is best for detecting alloantibodies hidden by the autoantibody?
options: Adsorption with selected reagent cells of known phenotypes
Treating the plasma with DTT to destroy the autoantibody
Repeating the panel using ficin-treated cells only
Prewarming the plasma and panel cells to 37 °C
items.why: Autoadsorption is not safe within about 3 months of transfusion, because transfused donor cells in the sample could also adsorb alloantibodies. **Allogeneic (differential) adsorption** uses reagent cells of known phenotypes (for example R1R1, R2R2, and rr, chosen for Kidd and other antigens) to remove the autoantibody while leaving alloantibodies that can then be identified.

whyNot.1: DTT breaks the disulfide bonds of IgM; it does not remove a warm IgG autoantibody.
whyNot.2: Enzymes usually make warm autoantibodies react more strongly and destroy some antigens (such as Fya), so the problem gets worse.
whyNot.3: Prewarming avoids cold-reacting antibodies; a warm IgG autoantibody still reacts at 37 °C.
