items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Autoimmune hemolytic anemias chapter; Detection and identification of antibodies chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: An antibody looks like anti-E. Under the standard rule for 95% confidence (p = 0.05), the minimum panel evidence needed is:
options: 1 E-positive cell that reacts and 1 E-negative cell that does not react
2 E-positive cells that react and 2 E-negative cells that do not react
6 E-positive cells that react, with no E-negative cells needed
3 E-positive cells that react and 3 E-negative cells that do not react
items.why: Using Fisher's exact method, the chance that 3 positive and 3 negative reactions would match an antigen pattern by accident is 1 in 20 (p = 0.05). So the usual rule is **3 antigen-positive reactive and 3 antigen-negative nonreactive cells**, using additional selected cells if the panel does not have enough.

whyNot.0: One positive and one negative cell could easily match the antigen pattern by chance (p = 0.5).
whyNot.1: Two and two gives p of about 0.17, which is not enough for 95% confidence.
whyNot.2: Without antigen-negative nonreactive cells, the specificity is not shown, and other antibodies are not ruled out.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Detection and identification of antibodies chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Donor units are being typed for Jka with commercial antiserum. Which cells make the best positive control?
options: Jk(a+b-) cells, which carry a double dose of Jka
Jk(a-b+) cells, which lack Jka
Jk(a+b+) cells, which carry a single dose of Jka
Red cells from the intended recipient
items.why: A positive control should show that the reagent can detect the weakest antigen expression expected. For antigens that show dosage, such as Kidd, **heterozygous Jk(a+b+) cells** are used as the positive control, and Jk(a-b+) cells are the negative control.

whyNot.0: Homozygous cells react strongly and would not show that the reagent can detect a weaker, single-dose antigen.
whyNot.1: Jk(a-b+) cells lack Jka and are the negative control.
whyNot.3: A recipient's Jka type is often unknown (and a patient who needs Jka-negative blood is Jka-negative), so these cells are not a reliable positive control.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Detection and identification of antibodies chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A fetus with anti-D HDFN is anemic but is not jaundiced at birth. Within hours of delivery, its unconjugated bilirubin rises quickly. Why does jaundice appear mainly after birth?
options: Maternal anti-D stops coating fetal cells once the cord is clamped
Before birth, bilirubin crosses the placenta and is cleared by the mother's liver
Fetal red cells are not hemolyzed until they are exposed to air
The fetal liver conjugates bilirubin well, but the newborn liver cannot
items.why: In utero, unconjugated bilirubin from hemolysis **crosses the placenta and is conjugated by the mother's liver**, so the fetus mainly shows anemia. After birth, the newborn's immature liver (low glucuronyl transferase) cannot keep up, and unconjugated bilirubin rises, with the risk of kernicterus.

whyNot.0: Maternal IgG stays in the infant's circulation for weeks after birth, so hemolysis continues.
whyNot.2: Hemolysis by maternal antibody happens in the fetal spleen before birth; air exposure has no role.
whyNot.3: Both fetal and newborn livers have limited conjugating ability; the difference is that the placenta is no longer there to clear bilirubin.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter

items.stem: A fetus with severe anemia from maternal anti-c needs an intrauterine transfusion. Which red cell unit is most suitable?
options: Group O, c-negative, irradiated, fresh, compatible with maternal plasma
Washed red cells from the father, since they match the fetus
Group AB, c-positive red cells stored at least 3 weeks
Fetal ABO/Rh-type cells crossmatched with the father's plasma
items.why: Blood for intrauterine transfusion must **lack the antigen of the maternal antibody and be compatible with the mother's plasma**, because her antibody is in the fetal circulation. It is usually group O, irradiated to prevent TA-GVHD, CMV-reduced-risk, HbS-negative, and as fresh as possible.

whyNot.1: The father's cells carry the c antigen the maternal antibody is directed against, which is why the fetus is affected.
whyNot.2: c-positive cells would be destroyed by the maternal anti-c; older units also have high potassium and low 2,3-DPG.
whyNot.3: The antibody causing the disease comes from the mother, so compatibility must be checked with her plasma, not the father's.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Four women have just delivered. Which one should receive postpartum Rh immune globulin (RhIG)? The mother is:
options: D-negative, with anti-D at titer 128 from earlier pregnancies
D-positive; her baby types D-negative on all testing
D-negative; baby lacks D even at the antiglobulin phase
D-negative; baby reacts with anti-D only at the AHG phase
items.why: RhIG is for a D-negative, unimmunized mother who may have been exposed to D-positive fetal cells. A baby whose cells react with anti-D only at the antiglobulin phase is weak D-positive, and **a weak D-positive infant counts as D-positive**, so the mother needs RhIG. It is not given once the mother has made her own (active) anti-D.

whyNot.0: A titer of 128 from earlier pregnancies shows active immunization; RhIG cannot reverse sensitization that has already happened.
whyNot.1: A D-positive mother cannot make anti-D, so RhIG is never needed.
whyNot.2: A D-negative baby, confirmed by weak D testing, cannot expose the mother to D, so RhIG is not needed after delivery.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: In older methods of monitoring HDFN, amniotic fluid was scanned with a spectrophotometer for the change in optical density at 450 nm (delta-OD450) and plotted on a Liley graph. What does this value estimate?
options: Free hemoglobin in the amniotic fluid
Fetal lung maturity (lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio)
Bilirubin pigment from fetal red cell destruction
Alpha-fetoprotein concentration
items.why: Bilirubin absorbs light at about 450 nm, so the rise in absorbance above the baseline at that wavelength reflects **amniotic fluid bilirubin**, an indirect measure of how much fetal hemolysis is happening. Results falling in higher Liley zones mean more severe disease; Doppler measurement of middle cerebral artery flow has now largely replaced this test.

whyNot.0: Hemoglobin absorbs most strongly near 410–415 nm (the Soret band); a peak there suggests contamination with blood.
whyNot.1: Lung maturity is assessed with lecithin/sphingomyelin and related tests, not absorbance at 450 nm.
whyNot.3: AFP is measured by immunoassay for neural tube defects, not by absorbance at 450 nm.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter

items.stem: Preoperative testing on a woman finds a positive DAT with anti-IgG only, but she is not anemic. An eluate from her red cells and her plasma react with all panel cells without any drug added, much like a warm autoantibody with Rh-related specificity. Which drug is most likely responsible?
options: High-dose IV penicillin
Quinine
Ceftriaxone
Methyldopa
items.why: Methyldopa induces a true red cell autoantibody that cannot be told apart serologically from a warm autoantibody: **the eluate and plasma react with normal red cells with no drug present**. A positive DAT develops in a sizeable minority of patients after several months of therapy, but few have hemolysis, and the antibody slowly disappears after the drug is stopped.

whyNot.0: Penicillin antibodies (drug adsorption mechanism) react only with penicillin-coated red cells, so the eluate does not react with normal panel cells.
whyNot.1: Quinine causes drug-dependent (immune complex type) antibodies that react only when the drug is present in the test, often with complement and acute intravascular hemolysis.
whyNot.2: Ceftriaxone antibodies are drug-dependent and react only in the presence of the drug; they can cause sudden, severe intravascular hemolysis.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia / Autoimmune hemolytic anemias chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A patient on very high-dose IV penicillin develops a positive DAT and slowly falling hemoglobin. Which laboratory finding best supports the drug adsorption (hapten) mechanism?
options: IgG eluate reacting with penicillin-treated cells but not untreated cells
DAT positive with anti-C3d only, with sudden intravascular hemolysis
An eluate that reacts with all panel cells, with or without the drug
Plasma that agglutinates cells only when penicillin is added to the tube
items.why: Penicillin binds firmly to red cell membrane proteins, and IgG anti-penicillin then binds to the drug on the cells. Because the antibody recognizes the drug on the membrane, the **eluate reacts only with drug-coated cells**, which defines the drug adsorption mechanism. Hemolysis is gradual and mostly extravascular.

whyNot.1: Complement-only coating with abrupt intravascular hemolysis fits the immune complex (drug-dependent) mechanism.
whyNot.2: Reactivity with all cells without the drug fits a drug-induced autoantibody, as with methyldopa.
whyNot.3: Needing the drug in solution with plasma and cells is typical of the immune complex mechanism; penicillin antibodies are shown with drug-coated cells.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A blood bank keeps several items for its refrigerator monitoring. Which one is a record?
options: The approved procedure for monitoring the refrigerator
Last month's temperature log, filled in and signed
A blank copy of the temperature log form
The facility's written quality policy
items.why: Quality systems separate documents, which say what to do or how to do it (policies, procedures, blank forms), from records, which show what was actually done. A **completed, signed log is a record**; the same form is a document while it is still blank.

whyNot.0: A procedure tells staff how to do the task; it is a document, not evidence that the task was done.
whyNot.2: A blank form is a controlled document; it becomes a record only after data are entered.
whyNot.3: A policy states what the facility intends to do; it is a document, not a record of work performed.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Quality management chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: Several samples arrive with mismatched labels. The technologist rejects them and asks for new samples, and she logs the event. The supervisor finds that labels were being printed in batches away from the patient, and she reports the occurrence to the quality unit. Which step is the corrective action?
options: Rejecting the samples and asking for new ones
Reporting the occurrence to the quality unit
Changing the procedure so labels are printed at the bedside
Logging the rejected samples in the occurrence log
items.why: Remedial action fixes the immediate problem, while corrective action removes the root cause so the problem does not happen again. **Changing the labeling procedure** addresses the root cause (batch printing), so it is the corrective action.

whyNot.0: Rejecting and recollecting the samples is the remedial action; it fixes these samples but does not stop the error from recurring.
whyNot.1: Reporting starts the occurrence management process, but it does not itself remove the cause.
whyNot.3: Logging creates a record of the event; it documents the problem but does not correct it.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Quality management chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: During validation of a blood bank computer system, a tester enters an ABO/D result: anti-A 4+, anti-B 0, anti-D 3+, A1 cells 4+, B cells 4+, with the interpretation 'group A, D-positive'. How should a correctly configured system respond?
options: Reject it: the reverse grouping does not fit group A
Accept it, since the forward grouping clearly shows group A
Accept it as group A2 with anti-A1 in the plasma
Reject it: anti-D reactions must be 4+ to be valid
items.why: Blood bank software checks each entry against a truth table that lists the valid combinations of reactions for every interpretation. Group A plasma should not agglutinate A1 cells, so **an entry whose forward and reverse groupings disagree must be rejected** and held as an unresolved ABO discrepancy rather than recorded as group A.

whyNot.1: The forward grouping alone does not establish the ABO group; a discrepancy with the reverse grouping must be resolved before a group is recorded.
whyNot.2: Anti-A1 in an A2 person usually reacts weakly and must be shown with anti-A1 lectin and A2 cells; the software cannot assign a subgroup while the discrepancy is unexplained.
whyNot.3: A 3+ anti-D reaction is a valid positive; the problem with this entry is the ABO discrepancy.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Informational systems in the blood bank chapter; ABO blood group system chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A blood sample spills on the bench in the blood bank. After absorbing the liquid, which disinfectant is recommended for the surface?
options: 1:1,000 dilution of household bleach
Detergent and water with no disinfectant
A sterile saline wipe-down
Freshly made 1:10 household bleach
items.why: Hepatitis B virus can stay infectious on dried surfaces for about a week, so spills need a disinfectant that kills it. A **freshly made 1:10 bleach (sodium hypochlorite) solution** with adequate contact time is the standard choice (an EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant is an alternative).

whyNot.0: A 1:1,000 dilution is too weak to reliably kill bloodborne viruses in a blood spill.
whyNot.1: Detergent cleans the surface but does not reliably kill HBV or other bloodborne pathogens.
whyNot.2: Saline has no disinfecting action.
